name: Sensitivity and specificity
seoDesc: Sensitivity and specificity: work out true positive from the false negative and the prevalence. A free statistics calculator with the formula, units and a…
summary: Supply the false negative, the prevalence, the positive likelihood ratio and the negative likelihood ratio and the Sensitivity and specificity calculator solves for true positive. That makes it useful for an assignment, a report or a data discussion where you need a defensible number. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Sensitivity and specificity calculator work?
sections.html:
The Sensitivity and specificity calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports true positive in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the false negative, the prevalence, the positive likelihood ratio and the negative likelihood ratio.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Sensitivity and specificity calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

True positive=-false negative × sensitivity ÷ (sensitivity − 1)
True negative=-false positive × specificity ÷ (specificity − 1)
Sensitivity=positive likelihood ratio × (1 − specificity)
Specificity=(1 − sensitivity) ÷ negative likelihood ratio
Sensitivity=positive predictive value (PPV) × (-prevalence × specificity + prevalence + specificity − 1) ÷ (prevalence × (positive predictive value (PPV) − 1))
Specificity=negative predictive value (NPV) × prevalence × (1 − sensitivity) ÷ (negative predictive value (NPV) × prevalence − negative predictive value (NPV) − prevalence + 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose False negative = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %. Working through the relationship above gives True positive = 1.1111.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: True positive = 1.1111 should be roughly the size you expected from False negative = 10 and Sensitivity = 10 %.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Sensitivity and specificity calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a result a piece of software produced
  • Deciding how much confidence a sample really supports
  • Turning raw numbers into something you can quote
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the false negative, the prevalence and the positive likelihood ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Sensitivity and specificity calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns true positive, derived from the false negative, the prevalence and the positive likelihood ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Sensitivity and specificity calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the false negative, the prevalence, the positive likelihood ratio and the negative likelihood ratio, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter prevalence in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Prevalence opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports True positive = 1.1111. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Sensitivity and specificity calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
